intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the peripherin/RDS gene (PRPH2) on chromosome 6p. Digenic RP7 is caused by double heterozygosity for mutations in the PRPH2 gene and the ROM1 gene. Homozygous mutation in PRPH2 has been reported in patients with early-onset retinal dystrophy with Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) or juvenile RP phenotypes.

checks.evidence_quote: Our results indicate that some cases of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa are due to mutations at the RDS locus.
checks.explanation: The abstract links RDS mutations to autosomal dominant RP. It does not use the RP7 designation or state that the mutations are heterozygous, although dominant inheritance implies this. Only the abstract was supplied.

checks.explanation: The abstract links the disease locus on 6p tightly to the peripherin gene, which places that gene on 6p.

checks.evidence_quote: Three families were identified with mutations in the unlinked photoreceptor-specific genes ROM1 and peripherin/RDS, in which only double heterozygotes develop retinitis pigmentosa (RP).
checks.explanation: The abstract says digenic RP comes from double heterozygosity for peripherin/RDS (PRPH2) and ROM1 mutations. Calling it 'RP7' is OMIM's labelling.

checks.evidence_quote: To our knowledge, our study reported for the first time that homozygous mutations in PRPH2 cause EORD with LCA/juvenile RP phenotypes.

paragraphs.text: Retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is an autosomal dominant retinal degeneration caused by mutation in the gene encoding the photoreceptor glycoprotein peripherin/RDS (PRPH2). PRPH2 mutations cause highly variable phenotypes, and retinitis pigmentosa, pattern macular dystrophy, and fundus flavimaculatus have been observed within a single family. A digenic form of RP occurs in individuals who are double heterozygotes for mutations in PRPH2 and ROM1.

checks.explanation: The abstract describes the disease caused by RDS mutations as autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa, a hereditary retinal degeneration.

paragraphs.text: Weleber et al. (1993) reported a family in which 3 separate phenotypes occurred. The 75-year-old mother presented at age 63 years with a profoundly abnormal electroretinogram (ERG) and adult-onset RP that progressed dramatically over 12 years, with marked loss of peripheral visual field. One daughter developed pattern macular dystrophy at age 31 years; at age 44 years her ERG was moderately abnormal, but her clinical disease was limited to the macula. Another daughter presented at age 42 years with macular degeneration and over 10 years developed the clinical picture of fundus flavimaculatus, with preserved peripheral visual field and a moderately abnormal ERG. The son had onset of macular degeneration at age 44 years, with pericentral scotomas, a markedly abnormal ERG, and punctate pigment epithelial transmission defects on fluorescein angiography.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2013) reported 3 patients with homozygous PRPH2 mutations who exhibited LCA or juvenile RP phenotypes, including visual impairment within the first year of life, nystagmus in the 2 patients with LCA, nondetectable or reduced ERGs, and a very similar form of maculopathy. Fundus findings included a multilobulated central atrophic maculopathy, concentric rings of yellow deposits, vessel narrowing, peripheral and macular pigment deposits, choroidal sclerosis, optic disc pallor, and retinal pigment epithelium mottling and loss. Heterozygous carrier relatives were asymptomatic but showed detectable maculopathy: the 56-year-old father of 1 patient had macular pattern dystrophy and clear-cut foveal changes with essentially normal visual acuity, and the 57-year-old mother of another patient had 20/20 visual acuity but a florid butterfly-shaped macular pattern dystrophy and a number of other retinal flecks.

paragraphs.text: Manes et al. (2015) found that the clinical severity of disease in French patients with autosomal dominant RP due to PRPH2 mutations was moderate, with 78% of eyes having 1-0.5 visual acuity and 52% of eyes retaining more than 50% of the visual field. Some patients characteristically showed vitelliform deposits or macular involvement. In some families, pericentral RP or macular dystrophy was found in some family members while widespread RP was present in other members of the same family.

paragraphs.text: By Sanger sequencing of PRPH2 in 310 French families with autosomal dominant RP, Manes et al. (2015) identified 15 mutations, including 6 novel and 9 previously reported changes, in 32 families. A recurrent novel mutation, leu254-to-gln (L254Q), led to protein aggregation when peripherin-2 was produced in yeast and analyzed by Western blot, suggesting abnormal folding.

checks.evidence_quote: PRPH2 was screened by Sanger sequencing in a cohort of 310 French families with adRP.

checks.evidence_quote: We identified 15 mutations, including 6 novel and 9 previously reported changes in 32 families

checks.evidence_quote: We identified 15 mutations, including 6 novel and 9 previously reported changes in 32 families

paragraphs.text: Wells et al. (1993) concluded that both RP and macular dystrophies are caused by mutations in RDS and that the functional significance of certain amino acids in peripherin-RDS may differ in cones and rods. Weleber et al. (1993) concluded that a single 3-bp deletion in PRPH2 can produce clinically disparate phenotypes even within the same family.

checks.evidence_quote: These findings demonstrate that both retinitis pigmentosa and macular dystrophies are caused by mutations in RDS

checks.evidence_quote: the functional significance of certain amino-acids in peripherin-RDS may be different in cones and rods.

checks.claim: Weleber et al. (1993) concluded that a single 3-bp deletion in PRPH2 can produce clinically disparate phenotypes even within the same family.
checks.evidence_quote: A 3-base pair deletion of codon 153 or 154 of the peripherin/RDS gene can produce clinically disparate phenotypes even within the same family.
checks.explanation: This is the paper's stated conclusion.

paragraphs.text: Manes et al. (2015) found that PRPH2 mutations accounted for 10.3% of autosomal dominant RP in a French cohort of 310 families, higher than previously reported (0% to 8%), making PRPH2 the second most frequent autosomal dominant RP gene after RHO in their series.

checks.evidence_quote: We identified 15 mutations, including 6 novel and 9 previously reported changes in 32 families, accounting for a prevalence of 10.3% in this adRP population.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly; the cohort was 310 French families.

checks.claim: The 10.3% frequency of PRPH2 mutations in French autosomal dominant RP found by Manes et al. (2015) was higher than previously reported frequencies of 0% to 8%.
checks.evidence_quote: The mutations in PRPH2 account for 10.3% of adRP in the French population, which is higher than previously reported (0%-8%)

checks.claim: In the Manes et al. (2015) French series, PRPH2 was the second most frequent autosomal dominant RP gene after RHO.
checks.evidence_quote: This makes PRPH2 the second most frequent adRP gene after RHO in our series.

Pigment deposits in periphery and macula
Visual impairment within first year of life (homozygous patients)

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2013) identified a homozygous c.554T-C transition in the PRPH2 gene, resulting in a leu185-to-pro (L185P) substitution at a residue conserved across species, in a patient with LCA (patient 3256) and in a patient with juvenile RP (patient 741). The mutation was found by targeted next-generation sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing; both parents of patient 741 were heterozygous, and the father had macular pattern dystrophy with essentially normal visual acuity. The authors noted that L185P, together with a null mutation in ROM1, had been reported to cause digenic RP.

checks.evidence_quote: we sequenced PRPH2 in another 135 unsolved LCA or juvenile RP patients and found the same homozygous missense mutation p.L185P in PRPH2 in a third juvenile RP patient, 741. These mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing
checks.explanation: Sanger confirmation is stated. Targeted NGS found the mutation in patient 3256, but patient 741 was identified by separate PRPH2 sequencing of 135 more patients, and the method is not specified as NGS.

checks.evidence_quote: the p.L185P mutation, together with a null mutation in ROM1, has been reported to cause digenic RP

paragraphs.text: In a patient with LCA (patient 1318), Wang et al. (2013) identified a homozygous c.637T-C transition in the PRPH2 gene, resulting in a cys213-to-arg (C213R) substitution at a residue conserved across species. The mutation, previously associated with autosomal dominant pattern dystrophy, was found by targeted next-generation sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Both parents and the patient's son were heterozygous, and a brother with normal vision was homozygous wildtype. The heterozygous mother, at 57 years of age, had 20/20 visual acuity but a florid butterfly-shaped macular pattern dystrophy, and the 7-year-old son had a miniature form of foveal butterfly-shaped macular pattern dystrophy.
